items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Zelenskyy rejects Trump's push to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy defended strikes on Russian oil facilities in an exclusive Fox News interview with Trey Yingst, saying Ukraine's response to Moscow's attacks "must be painful."
Russia played a larger role in the Iran war than previously disclosed, with internal defense industry documents revealing how Moscow built up the country's arsenal ahead of its conflict with the U.S.
A Russian contract is tied to 90 launchers for precision-guided missiles with the destination as Tehran, according to documents obtained and published by Ukrainian defense intelligence research group Dallas Analytics offering new details on the extent of Moscow's military support for Iran before war erupted.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly downplayed Russia's role in the conflict — as recently as last month, saying that he did not believe they are helping Iran "at all."
IRAN TAPS FINANCIAL LIFELINE, RUSSIAN ARMS AS TRUMP ESCALATES 'CRUSHING' ECONOMIC WARFARE
In this image released on July 4, 2026, Deputy Chairman of the Security Council of the Russian Federation Dmitry Medvedev shakes hands with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, and next to him are Chief Justice of Iran Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Eje’i and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi during a ceremony for the remains of Ayatollah Khamenei and his family at the Imam Khomeini Grand Mosque on July 3, 2026, in Tehran, Iran. (Meghdad Madadi ATPImages/Getty Images)
Russian production records show components were allocated for 90 APU-L twin-rail launchers under a contract identified as "K-10," with shipments within the Russian production chain scheduled from late 2024 through December 2025.
Other internal Russian documents obtained by Dallas Analytics explicitly identify "K-10" as Iran. An October 2022 supply request for equipment for a Yak-130 aircraft lists the consignee as "'K10' Iran" and was countersigned by the acting head of the Russian Defense Ministry's 704th Military Representation.
The K-10 designation can also be traced to Russian military hardware that ultimately reached Iran. An internal Russian production schedule listed six Yak-130 aircraft for a consignee identified as K-10. Iranian state media later showed the aircraft entering service in September 2023, and Dallas Analytics said the tail number of one Iranian Yak-130 matched the number listed for K-10 in the Russian factory records.
The APU-L launchers are designed to carry Russia's LMUR, a precision-guided missile also known as Product 305 or the Kh-39. The roughly 230-pound missile carries a 55-pound warhead and can be guided in flight by an operator using an electro-optical seeker and two-way radio link.
A missile is launched during an air defense drill in an undisclosed location in Iran in a handout image from Jan. 12, 2025. (Iranian Army/West Asia News Agency/Reuters)
FOREIGN LEADER ON PUTIN’S DOORSTEP SOUNDS ALARM OVER IRAN FUELING MOSCOW’S WAR MACHINE
Iran had already publicly announced plans to acquire Russian Mi-28 attack helicopters, one of the platforms capable of carrying the weapon. The first export-variant Mi-28NE helicopters were photographed in Iran in January 2026.
The paperwork also shows involvement by Russia's Defense Ministry. A May 2024 letter accompanying the K-10 production schedule was co-signed by the head of the ministry's 123rd Military Representation.
The documents do not establish whether the completed launchers ultimately reached Iran, though Dallas Analytics told Fox News Digital the contract itself is "a very strong proof" of the transfer.
SATELLITE IMAGES MAY HAVE TIPPED OFF IRAN BEFORE US BASE ATTACK, TOP REPUBLICAN WARNS
The findings add new detail to a military relationship the Trump administration has repeatedly played down during the war. U.S. intelligence has assessed that Russia provided Iran with information on the location of American military assets and, more recently, satellite imagery and weapons components, according to reports.
But administration officials have said that support has not materially affected the U.S. campaign.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Russian assistance was not impeding U.S. military operations, while Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has said the U.S. was tracking Moscow's support and accounting for it in its battle plans.
The remains of a Russian-made, Iran-designed Shahed-136 drone, known in Russia as a Geran-2, are displayed with other recovered drones, glide bombs, missiles and rockets in Kharkiv on July 30, 2025. (Scott Peterson/Getty Images)
The Trump administration has separately sought to disrupt Iran's foreign weapons procurement as Tehran works to rebuild its military capabilities.
The Treasury Department has targeted networks it says helped Iran seek weapons and components abroad, including efforts to acquire Chinese-made man-portable air-defense systems.
Just this week, the State Department sanctioned a Russia-based individual it said was involved in efforts to help Iran procure Chinese-made man-portable air-defense systems, or MANPADS.
Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House, State Department and Department of War for comment.

items.title: Nvidia tightens tracking of AI GPUs in Southeast Asia as Chinese chip smuggling draws scrutiny, report claims — cloud providers must join monitoring program to qualify for official partner status - Tom's Hardware
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Southeast Asia computing providers are now reportedly required to register with Nvidia's Fleet Intelligence tracking system if they want to become official Nvidia Cloud Partners (NCPs). The move, according to Bloomberg , is aimed at giving the chipmaker another way to monitor where its AI accelerators are deployed, as Washington grows increasingly frustrated with restricted hardware finding its way into China through regional smuggling networks. Nvidia was not immediately available for comment.
Go deeper with TH Premium: Taiwan, trade, and tariffs
While the U.S. flip-flops on chip sanctions, China is building its own chip supply market
The state of China's decade-long semiconductor push
China's CXMT targets 30% DRAM memory market share by 2030 with sixth mega-fab
China's latest round of rare-earth export controls explained
The NCP designation is worth pursuing as it gives cloud providers Nvidia's public endorsement and preferred access to its sought-after AI chips, putting the company in a position to use those benefits as leverage. Customers seeking the status must now enroll in Fleet Intelligence , according to people familiar with the new requirements. Fleet Management was introduced last December primarily as a data centre management tool. It gathers information about NVIDIA hardware deployed across participating companies' infrastructure, including the locations of individual accelerators. That information could give Nvidia a better picture of whether its chips are operating after they leave the supply chain.
The system is, however, a universal tracking mandate. Participation has remained voluntary outside the NCP requirement, and Nvidia does not automatically receive location data from every customer using the software. The company has also not clarified whether existing Cloud Partners will have to enroll to retain their designation or whether the requirement will eventually extend beyond Southeast Asia.
Notably, Nvidia has been developing a way to locate AI for some time now. Last December, we reported that the company had developed software-based GPU tracking , using GPU telemetry and network latency measurements to estimate where processors are operating. Nvidia described the software as a customer-installed agent for monitoring hardware health, integrity and inventory.
The technology has an obvious use beyond data maintenance. The U.S. restricts Chinese companies from purchasing advanced AI accelerators without a license, yet authorities believe billions of dollars worth of the hardware have reached Chinese buyers through third-party networks, with Southeast Asia becoming an important transit point for those transactions.
A C4ADS investigation has previously identified several routes used to move restricted processors into China, including purchases through research initiatives, shell companies and shipments routed through other Southeast Asian countries. The nonprofit examined transactions between 2022 and 2025 and identified $13.4 million worth of Nvidia A100, H100, and AD102-series GPUs moving through regional trade routes. Its report also linked $4.6 billion in hardware purchases to Singapore-based Megaspeed International.
Megaspeed has become a particularly awkward case for Nvidia, with the company being under U.S. and Singaporean investigation for more than a year over suspected chip diversion. Last week, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang defended his dealings with the firm, describing them as "completely normal," adding, "we've studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one." Megaspeed denied any wrongdoing. In April, Megaspeed's Malysisan data centre landlord terminated its contract, reallocating 68.4 megawatts of capacity to another cloud provider

Moreover, Megaspeed is not the only example of how difficult it can be to police the movement of AI hardware. Earlier this year, U.S. prosecutors accused people associated with Super Micro of helping divert around $2.5 billion worth of Nvidia-powered servers to China through Southeast Asian intermediaries. The alleged scheme involved falsified paperwork and dummy server shells, with genuine hardware shipped onward after inspections. More recently, the company has faced additional scrutiny over its export compliance after inspections. Nvidia has also reportedly removed half of the Asian companies on its pre-approved buyer list and told cloud providers to keep at least 51% of their computing services with customers outside China.

items.title: Spain's rail authorities face European fraud probe after Urda rail disaster
items.summary: Prosecutors begin investigating EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people.
items.content:
Image caption, Last month's train crash in which 69 people died was the second deadly accident on the same high-speed line this year
European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds meant for upgrading the Spanish railway line where a train crash killed 69 people last week.
Prosecutors backed by a special unit of Spain's Guardia Civil security force said they were conducting the inquiry at the offices of Adif rail infrastructure authority and rail safety agency AESF.
The 28 October accident on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.
It is the second EU fraud inquiry opened into Spain's railways this year, after 46 people were killed on the same line at Adamuz in January.
Last week, a train operated by state-owned operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The LZB communication system that monitors the position of trains had gone down, and the Renfe train had been given the all clear to start running at normal speed, even though the Iryo train ahead of it had been unable to restart.
The two accidents nine months apart on the same line have claimed 115 lives and dozens more injuries.
Shock of rail tragedy gives way to sorrow and outrage in politically divided Spain
Spanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash
The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) said on Friday it had begun conducting investigative measures at Spain's rail authorities "after the opening of an investigation into possible fraud affecting EU funds , external allocated to the renovation and upgrading of safety, signalling and communications systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed railway line".
The EPPO highlighted high public interest in the case, but said no further details would be made public.
As part of the process, a Spanish judge assigned to the case has to ensure the investigation complies with legal safeguards, including authorising any measures that might involve house searches or phone-tapping.
Image caption, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez (C) faces parliamentary elections on 29 November
The Urda disaster has damaged the Socialist-led government of Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez ahead of a 29 November general election and the party is trailing the conservative People's Party (PP) in most opinion polls.
Close SÃ¡nchez ally Ãscar Puente resigned this week as transport minister, after seeing two deadly accidents on his watch this year.
The PP and far-right Vox say Puente's resignation is not enough and they have demanded that SÃ¡nchez resign too.
Many people in Spain have now become wary of taking the train, with reports of widespread cancellations and empty station platforms.
A funeral for the 69 victims at Urda will take place on Tuesday at Toledo cathedral, in the same province that the disaster happened.
Puente's successor, Carlos Cuerpo, has vowed to take all necessary measures to "restore the confidence of Spaniards in our high-speed rail".
Cuerpo met survivors of January's Adamuz disaster on Friday and they handed him a list of 11 demands for improving safety on Spain's railways.

items.content:
If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett Says This Is the Wisest Move You Can Make
Over the long haul, the U.S. stock market has been one of the greatest wealth creation machines in history. And the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has recently taken things into overdrive, with the benchmark S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) soaring 115% since the release of OpenAI's ChatGPT in late 2022. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) has performed even better, rising 150%.
But roller-coaster rides are just as scary as they are exhilarating. And the previous decades of financial history show that severe drawdowns have often followed similar periods of explosive equity growth. No one knows this better than investing legend Warren Buffett.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Let's explore what could happen next in the stock market, using Buffett's advice as a guide on what investors should do to stay ahead.
There are many methods investors use to gauge how expensive stocks are relative to other periods in history. But the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio is one of the most useful, as it accounts for inflation and the business cycle to reduce the impact of short-term fluctuations in corporate earnings.
Right now, the S&P 500 trades at a CAPE ratio of 40.1, well above its historic average of 17.4. This is important because the metric has only spiked above 32.6 twice in history. The first was in 1929, right before the stock market crash that led to the Great Depression. And the second time was in late 1999, when it peaked at 44.2 shortly before the dot-com bubble burst, and the market entered a multiyear decline.
The current generative AI situation has stark similarities to the dot-com bubble because both were sparked by a transformative new technology. But whether they end the same remains to be seen.
A November Barron's survey found that only 37% of professional investors believe that current AI infrastructure spending will produce positive returns in two years. It's easy to see why people are getting pessimistic.
According to The Wall Street Journal , U.S. consumers and businesses will have to spend $3.5 trillion annually by 2032 to justify the capital currently being invested in the opportunity. This is roughly 8.8% of gross domestic product (GDP), which sounds like a tall order because it would put spending ahead of essentials like energy and almost at the level of food.
Eventually, hyperscalers may come to realize they are spending money they may not recoup while also cannibalizing their high-margin software revenue in favor of new, highly uncertain growth drivers. These issues recently came to a head at Alphabet , which saw its stock price fall by almost 13% shortly after third-quarter earnings revealed rising AI spending coupled with slowing growth in the search business.
Image source: Getty Images. With over six decades of investing experience, Warren Buffett is no stranger to booms and busts. He navigated the dot-com bubble and the Great Recession, as well as multiple financial crises in the 1970s and 1980s. But one of his remarks during a 1999 interview with Fortune Magazine might be the most relevant to the situation today:
The key to investing is not assessing how much an industry will affect society or how much it will grow, but rather determining the competitive advantage of any given company and, above all, the durability of that advantage. Products or services with wide, sustainable moats deliver rewards to investors.
The lesson is to avoid the temptation of unquestioningly jumping into every fast-growing AI stock. While many of these companies are doing well now, they may struggle to hold on to their market shares as the industry matures and competition intensifies over the long haul.

items.title: Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions? - Al Jazeera
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Share Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions? on social media
Vessels at the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, November 3, 2026 [Stringer/Reuters]
Iran has exempted ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar from its Strait of Hormuz restrictions, a senior Iranian lawmaker said on Tuesday.
“Ships from these countries pass freely, and the Americans do not intercept them either,” Amir Hayat Moqaddam, deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA).
list of 4 items list 1 of 4 US sanctions Indian and Turkish firms accused of helping Iran
list 2 of 4 Congress defeat: How Trump’s allies are distancing themselves from Iran war
list 3 of 4 Iran, Gaza, Ukraine: What will US midterm results mean for these conflicts?
list 4 of 4 ‘Knives out’: Will Congress impeach Pete Hegseth after GOP midterms loss?
Iran effectively shut the strait early in the US-Israel war on Iran , which began on February 28, and the United States reimposed a naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports in July.
So why have these four countries been granted passage through the critical strait, and can their ships really sail freely while the blockade remains in place?
What does Iran get in return for letting ships pass?
It will receive medicine from India and political backing from China, according to Hayat Moqaddam. Iran already receives diplomatic support from Qatar, which is leading mediation efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran.
Hayat Moqaddam said Tehran will also collect transit fees from Indian and Chinese ships, while Qatari vessels pass free. He did not say whether Iraqi ships will pay a toll.
“Whatever the lawmaker says is the rationale – the big question is if it works and, if yes, to what extent?” Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, told Al Jazeera.
“Iran has been under sanctions for a very long time, so bartering and quid pro quos in trade are nothing new,” he said. The difference now, he added, is that “it’s about poking holes in an embargo and getting crucial goods/services in and out”.
Nader Hashemi, an associate professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, said that “most likely Iran is charging a transit fee or a percentage of the cargo value to allow those ships to go through without being harassed”.
“It’s a clever move by Tehran for several reasons,” Wolfgang Pusztai, a security and defence analyst and Austria’s former defence attache to Libya, told Al Jazeera.
“If successful, this move will generate significant revenue for Iran, as China is by far the largest purchaser of Iranian crude oil, buying nearly 90 percent of Iran’s total oil exports,” he said.
By including Qatar, with its many liquefied natural gas (LNG) buyers, and India, Iran is also “trying to undermine acceptance” of Washington’s strategy in the conflict, especially as it charges Qatar no tolls, he added.
All four are highly dependent on the Strait of Hormuz for exports.
Of the 10.23 million barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42 percent went to China and 13 percent to India, Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler, told Al Jazeera.
“China is the country most able to cross US interests. The question is whether Beijing considers it worth the potential political cost,” Parsi said.
Asia is particularly reliant on Gulf oil and gas usually shipped out via Hormuz. Countries there have much to offer in return for allowing ships to pass.
“For India, the shutdown of oil from the Gulf has been a great loss – and it is a big producer of the pharmaceuticals that Iran cannot manufacture itself,” he said.
Qatar, which is mediating between Washington and Tehran, shipped no LNG through the strait in August, but managed 1.8 million tonnes in October, Xu said.
Its crude transits fell over the same period, from 517,000 barrels a day to 193,000, while Iraq’s rose from 1.69 million to 2.65 million.
Kpler has been unable to trace the origin of up to two million barrels a day of Middle Eastern crude, so both countries’ flows may be higher, Xu said.
“India and Qatar have closer relationships with DC they need to maintain – while both of them also feel let down by Trump,” Parsi said, adding, “For Qatar, maintaining a relationship with Iran is also vital since it’s an unavoidable neighbour.”
“So for all of them, there are upsides for these exemptions from Iranian restrictions but also political dangers,” he said.
Iran began letting some vessels from countries it considers friendly pass within weeks of the war starting. And in April, its military command said “brotherly” Iraq was exempt.
With the Iraqi exemption, Iran “probably intends to support the economic recovery” of its western neighbour, a fellow Shia-majority country, Pusztai said.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) has said the blockade applies to “all vessels of all nations entering or leaving coastal areas or ports in Iran”, while vessels avoiding Iranian ports are not affected.
It has also said humanitarian shipments, including “food and medical supplies essential for the survival of the civilian populations”, can pass after inspection.
But Hayat Moqaddam did not appear to limit the exemptions to ships trading with other Gulf states, Pusztai noted. “If this is really the case, this would also have a significant impact on the other Gulf states, including Saudi Arabia,” he said.
“This could make the continuation of the American naval blockade more difficult and less effective, assuming Washington accepts this Iranian move,” he said. The main change, he added, is that the exemption “would also cover Chinese/Indian ships from/to Iran”, if the US accepts it.
It is also unclear whether “ships of these countries” means the flag a vessel flies, its owner, its operator or some other link, Pusztai said.
Ending the blockade is one of Tehran’s demands before it will commit to broader peace talks with the US, which will include discussions about Iran’s nuclear programme. Qatar-mediated talks currently centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait if the US meets seven conditions, including this and lifting sanctions.
“It seems to be that Iran tries to separate the questions of free passage through the Strait of Hormuz and oil exports from the nuclear question,” Pusztai said, adding, “The American reaction will show if this is successful.”
“I think they make only limited difference at present,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera.
“Markets are back to pricing in a peace deal, but if conflict flares up at full tilt, then Iranian commanders may not have time to distinguish their targets,” he said, adding: “At present, the focus remains squarely on the prospects of a broader deal.”
An exemption has not guaranteed safety. On October 30, the Qatari LNG carrier Al Mayeda was struck by “unidentified objects” in the Gulf, said its owner, Qatar Gas Transport Company.
More than 120 commercial ships have been hit in the region since the war began, with October being the worst month, according to data from the International Maritime Organization and United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.

Wall Street's "energy transition" funds hold natural gas and data center companies, and Blackstone calls gas essential to the transition.

As we head into the United Nations’ 31st annual flagship climate conference (COP31), to be held next week in Antalya, Türkiye, greenwashing presents a large and growing problem in the private sector. As the tech sector’s greenhouse gas emissions explode against the backdrop of the artificial intelligence boom and the clean energy incentives dry up under the Trump administration, Big Tech and Wall Street alike are funding a boom in natural gas, all under the guise of funding the future of clean energy.
“ On Wall Street, the ‘energy transition’ includes natural gas and data centers ,” blared a Grist headline published earlier this week. The article details how private equity funds are making a killing on “energy transition” funds as electrification takes hold on a global scale and solar and wind power continue to see runaway growth trends, both current and projected. But many of these prominent energy transition funds prominently feature a fossil fuel and major contributors to greenhouse gas emissions on a global scale: natural gas.
“‘Energy transition’ is a flexible term,” says Dan Cohn, an energy finance analyst with the energy think tank Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. “And I’m unsurprised to see either the gas or electrical equipment and data center-related companies in some of these funds. That is perfectly consistent with how I know some investors think about the energy transition,” he went on to say.
And those investors are not alone. Natural gas has been heavily promoted by the fossil fuel sector as a ‘bridge fuel’, serving as a stepping stone in the transition away from oil and coal toward 100 percent renewables. However, environmental experts question the wisdom of this approach and scientists have pushed back on the idea that natural gas is any cleaner than other fossil fuels, and calls for the abandonment of the ‘bridge fuel’ narrative have gained momentum in recent years.
Methane, the principal ingredient in natural gas, is an extremely potent greenhouse gas. While methane breaks up much more quickly in the atmosphere than the better-known carbon dioxide, it is 80 times more potent at warming over a 20-year period. And peer–reviewed studies (like this one , this one , and this one ) are increasingly indicating that natural gas produces much, much more methane over its life cycle than previously thought. Plus, some studies even indicate that natural gas could be worse for the climate than coal when you include the emissions associated with the energy-intensive cooling, storage, and shipping processes associated with liquefied natural gas.
However, the ‘bridge fuel’ argument still seems to hold major currency on Wall Street and in Silicon Valley. “I know a lot of the investors out there do consider gas a transition fuel,” Ryan Loughead, a senior associate and former climate solutions analyst for BloombergNEF, told Grist. For example, New York-based Blackstone, one of the world’s largest private equity firms, “is explicit in its view that methane gas, a fossil fuel and the primary component of natural gas, is essential to the energy transition,” reports Grist.
Meanwhile, Big Tech firms are causing a major natural gas boom around the country at the same time that they tout their backing of next-gen clean energy research, development, and adoption. Some of the biggest names in tech are building historically huge natural gas plants as we speak. Amazon is constructing a gas-fired power plant in Texas that will be the single-biggest source of power-related emissions in the entire United States according to current specs, which include seven gas plants. And in August, Nvidia announced that it would partner with Japan’s SoftBank and the federal government to build the largest fossil-fuel plant in the United States to power an Ohio project by OpenAI, the firm behind ChatGPT. And Microsoft just signed a 20-year deal with Chevron to provide 2.67 gigawatts of natural-gas fired power for a proposed West Texas data center.
Together, these developments greatly imperil the world’s ability to keep global warming within manageable limits. The United Nations says that it is now an inevitability that the world will fail to meet the legally binding goals set forth by the Paris climate accord as a result of “ decades of insufficient climate action ”, but notes that here is “ample opportunity to accelerate action”, and concludes that “countries can still limit peak warming, shorten the duration of overshoot and keep the goals of the Paris Agreement within reach”. Removing natural gas as a pillar of transition agendas and portfolios is clearly one such opportunity.

Fed's Mary Daly says higher interest rates 'are likely to be needed' in inflation fight
San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said in a CNBC interview Friday that she expects the central bank will have to raise benchmark interest rates further as it battles inflation.
On the labor market, she said Friday's jobs report was "good news for American workers" who nevertheless are seeing wages that are not keeping up with inflation.
San Francisco Fed president on jobs report: This is good news for American workers
San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly said Friday she expects the central bank will need to raise interest rates further, but joined her fellow policymakers in saying the pace and timing remain uncertain.
"My expectation is we're going to have to tighten policy further. Exactly when and how much is still to be decided because we just have to take all the variables that are coming in," Daly told CNBC's Steve Liesman during a live interview. "More is likely to be needed, and certainly ... I'm prepared to do that if that's what the economy calls for."
The remarks came the same day the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October while the unemployment rate — the labor-market variable Fed officials focus on most — edged lower to 4.1%.
Those numbers were substantially better than Wall Street expectations. Job creation, in fact, was nearly triple the Dow Jones consensus estimate.
Daly called the report "good news for American workers," but noted the pressure inflation is exerting on household finances. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% annually in October, but the September inflation rate as measured by the consumer price index was 3.7%.

"They see that they can get jobs, they continue to spend. They're not out of the game, but they are on a treadmill of high inflation," she said. "This has been high for too long, almost six years, and we're really starting to feel the burden of that spread everywhere."
The policymaker said she's not concerned generally about economic growth but worried about the persistence of inflation.
"The job market remains stable and solid, but not booming, and you see real wages falling because those wages are not really keeping up with inflation," Daly said. "I think that's the crux of this. Good news on the jobs front, not so clear that Americans are going to gain ground in the labor market."
The rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee in September increased the central bank's benchmark overnight borrowing rate by a quarter percentage point to a target range of 3.75%-4%.
However, the committee last week declined to follow up that hike with another move, saying it preferred to wait for "the accumulation of more information" before deciding its next move.
Daly will vote on the committee next year and said she still favors a gradual approach. Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin said Thursday he also sees higher rates ahead but is unsure of the timeline.
"I was really supportive and completely thought that that was the right move to move in September," Daly said. "I also think that it was good to be on hold at the last meeting because the world is filled with uncertainty."

European airlines have again been hit with a new wave of bomb threats - in the third such incident this week.
On Friday multiple flights to and from Lisbon, Rome, Prague and Sofia were targeted and the threats saw three planes escorted by Hungarian fighter jets, authorities said.
It also saw a number of high-profile media organisations, including Ireland's public broadcaster RTÃ , evacuated after threats were made against them - although there has been no concrete links between the messages against airlines and the broadcasters.
The disruption comes after nearly 30 aircraft and several airports across Europe were impacted by threats earlier this week , in what the UK called a "malicious hoax".
Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats
A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, according to AFP.
France also reported at least four of its flights were targeted by threats, however they all landed safely.
No explosives have been found on any planes as of Friday.
As airlines were dealing with this latest wave of threats, several media outlets, including RTÃ, were evacuated after similar warnings were made against them.
Staff at the Irish Independent newspaper and the Dublin offices of radio stations NewstalkFM and TodayFM, were also advised to leave their buildings and UK broadcaster Sky said it also received a security threat.
In a statement, gardaÃ­ (Irish police) said they were "aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe".
Image caption, Armed gardaÃ­ were deployed to RTÃ'S Dublin headquarter after a bomb threat
While no link has been established between the threats against airlines and media outlets, the Irish government has warned it is a "likely coordinated campaign of disruption".
In a statement, it said: "Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or co-ordinated effort.
Irish Prime Minister MicheÃ¡l Martin described the situation as "worrying" and added his government's first priority was the safety of the Irish public.
"Yesterday, there appeared to be coordinated efforts to disrupt air travel," he said.
Martin told RTÃ it was not yet known if the threats had come from individuals or if it was a "coordinated attack" but said they were being taken seriously.
Ireland is scheduled to host two high-profile European Union meetings in Dublin next week.
Broadcaster Sky confirmed it had received a security threat, hours after RTÃ had evacuated its building.
The broadcaster, which is owned by Comcast, said in a statement read by a presenter on its news channel that the broadcaster had "carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities".
"The safety and security of our colleagues is our primary concern, and we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure."
Friday's disruption comes after the Russian extremist group "Male State", named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, denied any link to the false warnings .
Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.
"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"

How many Russian soldiers died in the war with Ukraine
Mediazona , working with the  BBC’s  Russian service and a team of volunteers, has been compiling and maintaining a named list of the Russian military dead. The list is built from publicly available, verifiable sources, such as social media posts by relatives, reports in local media, and statements from regional authorities. Of course, this list is not exhaustive, as not every death is publicly reported.
To build a more complete picture of the war’s true toll, we have developed an estimate based on excess male mortality, using data from the national Probate Registry. This statistical method, created in collaboration with  Meduza , helps to account for the limitations of relying solely on publicly reported deaths.
Bi-weekly Summary. A text summary, updated every two weeks, in which we report on what we have learned about recent losses and the frontline events that led to the deaths of Russian soldiers.
Interactive Infographics. The second part provides visualisations of the losses since the start of the war, showing, for example, where the dead served or which regions they came from. We update the data for these graphics, while the accompanying text is refreshed but remains largely the same.
A detailed description of our method for estimating total deaths using Probate Registry data can be found at this link .

On March 8, 2022, Vladimir Putin said that “conscripts and reservists will not participate in the special military operation,” Russian government’s preferred (and brutally enforced) term for the war in Ukraine.
“Let me emphasize:conscripted soldiers are not participating and will not participate in combat operations, and there will be no additional call-up of reservists. Only professional military personnel are carrying out the assigned tasks,” he said at the time.
As we now know,the promise regarding an “additional call-up of reservists” lasted only until the announcement of “partial mobilisation” in September 2022, half a year into the invasion. Conscripts, meanwhile, ended up in the war immediately: we know that at least three conscripts were killed as early as February 24, 2022.
By March 9, Putin instructed the military prosecutor’s office to investigate how conscripts had ended up in the combat zone. Despite this, conscripts continued to serve in the war: on paper, the Ministry of Defence divided military units into those “participating” and “not participating” in the “special military operation”. One unit designated as “not participating in the SMO” was the guided-missile cruiser Moskva: out of 28 killed and missing, 20 were conscripts.
From May 2022 until August 2024, monthly casualties among conscripts rarely exceeded 10 men.
Everything changed in early August 2024, when the Ukrainian Armed Forces launched an incursion into the Kursk region. The chart clearly shows how sharply casualties among conscripts rose immediately after this date.
While the losses in August 2024 could be explained by the surprise nature of the Ukrainian attack on units considered “rear-echelon” and relatively safe, the deaths of dozens of conscripts between September and February no longer fit that logic: our data shows that conscripts were deliberately kept in the combat zone in the Kursk region.
In total, we have confirmed the deaths of at least 350 conscripts over the course of the entire war so far. These were definitively conscripts: they had not signed contracts with the Ministry of Defence, and volunteers specifically cross-checked every single record to verify this. We decided to publish this list separately.
Before the war began, conscripts served as the primary source for replenishing the ranks of the “professional military” Putin spoke of. Young men were pressured into signing three-year contracts. Once the war started, the situation shifted: most new soldiers now sign contracts as “volunteers” in exchange for payouts or are recruited from prisons.
However, pressure on conscripts has also intensified, and they are increasingly coerced into signing contracts. Although nominally “one-year” contracts, they are effectively indefinite—remaining in force until the “partial mobilisation” decree ends.
Currently,our records include at least 668 killed soldiers who signed a contract during their mandatory military service. This is a minimum baseline; the true figure is significantly higher. As the chart illustrates, the bulk of these losses also occurred during the Ukrainian incursion into the Kursk region, and casualties have remained high even after April 2025, when fighting on Russian territory had already ended.
Given that data for 2026 is the most incomplete (and “former conscripts” is one of the hardest categories to verify), we may uncover even higher casualty figures in the future among those coerced into signing contracts during their mandatory service.

The Nasdaq Composite plunged 5.5% on Thursday, closing in correction territory, defined as a decline of 10% or more from a recent closing high.
Fears of a crackdown on data centers sent tech stocks spiraling after Texas elected a new governor, Gina Hinojosa, who had promised a temporary moratorium on data centers until new rules can be applied to them to ensure that they are not extractive.

A full-on backlash against data centers seems unlikely, and there's always the possibility that they could move to neighboring states or even outside the country. AI demand is strong enough that new capacity will be created somewhere.
Thursday's crash was also a gut check for investors, and a reminder that sentiment can change quickly. AI stocks have skyrocketed this year, after all, and a number of them have doubled or better, even after Thursday's retreat. Much of those gains were driven by sentiment, so they are easily given back once that reverses.
For investors looking for some counsel at a time like this, the words of Warren Buffett are always a good source and a reminder to take a long-term view. In fact, not long ago, Buffett offered three words of advice that seem appropriate now.
Market corrections happen on average about every 18 months. In other words, they are a normal part of the investment cycle, and investors should be prepared for them.
Back in March, after the U.S. had launched the war in Iran, the S&P 500 was approaching a correction, and longtime Berkshire Hathaway CEO Warren Buffett was asked about it on CNBC. "Three times since I've taken over Berkshire, it's gone down more than 50%," he replied. "This is nothing."
Buffett was sitting on a pile of cash at the time, as Berkshire still is, and his comment implied that the sell-off wasn't enough to start deploying that capital.
Buffett's words turned out to be prescient as the market soon bounced back, ripping higher and, in less than a month, was back at all-time highs.
Buffett's advice is a reminder that while it may be painful to lose 5% of your portfolio in a single session, it's not a reason to panic. A 5% pullback in a single day is severe, but pullbacks are a normal part of investing, and making emotional decisions is the wrong move.
The stock market is also unpredictable in the short term, and Buffett's comment preceding a huge rally is a reminder that stocks could bounce off of Thursday's sell-off in the coming days or weeks.
There's another Warren Buffett expression that seems appropriate at the moment as well. Buffett famously counseled: "Be greedy when others are fearful, and fearful when others are greedy.
Thursday's sell-off looks like a lot of fear driven by the data center issue, which comes on the heels of concerns about high interest rates and large capital expenditures, which had also driven the sector lower.
It's worth remembering that despite concerns about a bubble, the tech stocks at the center of the AI boom continue to deliver strong results on the top and bottom lines, and valuations still look very reasonable. Nvidia now trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of less than 23, and Meta Platforms trades at a P/E of just 20.
These stocks look oversold and undervalued, and there are others like them. The current pullback might not be a steep enough sell-off to intrigue Buffett, but those are great prices to pay for high-quality stocks. Investors should keep their focus on the long term and take advantage of dips on top stocks.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again
In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you'd invested $5,000 then, you'd be sitting on $2,601,484 today.*
Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It's a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast.

items.title: Major construction ongoing near Iran missile bases, satellite images suggest
items.summary: Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November, satellite images suggest.
items.content:
By Shayan Sardarizadeh ,Â  Benedict Garman Â  and Â  Matt Murphy ,Â  BBC Verify
Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its major missile sites and repairing bases damaged by months of US and Israeli air strikes, analysis of satellite images suggests.
Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November at the Garmdareh military base in Karaj near the capital Tehran and the Shahroud base in the north, analysts at British intelligence company MAIAR, who reviewed the photos, told BBC Verify.
At least 12 other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases, appear to show signs of repairs. New roofs have been built on destroyed buildings at the Kermanshah missile base in western Iran, near the border with Iraq, while damaged buildings and debris have been cleared at the Parchin military complex - which has been repeatedly repaired despite a succession of air strikes - east of the capital.
The excavations near Shahroud could potentially be related to the production of missiles, said Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst who focused on Iran. He said that because the nearby air base at Shahroud has been targeted multiple times in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is probably trying to find ways to move its production facilities underground.
A MAIAR analyst said that Iran has "a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to protect them from further strikes". Mark Mellett, a defence analyst and former head of the Irish military, said the construction of underground facilities had the added benefit of making it "harder for outside observers to assess the extent and operational status".
Speculation has mounted in recent weeks that the US could resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections held earlier this week. But on Wednesday Vice-President JD Vance cited the war's unpopularity with voters for the Republicans' poor performance in this week's poll, saying that it may have cost his party control of the Senate "for the next 6 years".
At multiple bases across the country, Iranian forces have focused on carrying-out small-scale repairs to complexes which have been heavily damaged by air strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war.
Analysts said that satellite images appear to show that significant construction has been completed at the Taleghan 2 facility at the Parchin military complex, with damaged buildings levelled and the aftermath of attacks on an underground bunker repaired and reinforced with concrete.
At Karaj , external and Shahroud, satellite images appear to show significant excavation. At Karaj, multiple vehicles were visible in satellite images, while improvements appear to have been carried out to the nearby airbase.
The images from Karaj appear to show "a new portal for an underground facility", said Sam Lair, research analyst at the Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI), which has looked extensively into recent developments at Iranian sites.
Analysis from Janes also indicates there appears to be a new facility under construction at Karaj, including tunnel entrances and structures which could indicate an expansion of nearby damaged or destroyed missile bases - or could also be for storage or other purposes.
The construction work is unlikely to be part of an effort to deceive foreign intelligence agencies, said Janes analyst Sean O'Connor. He said such a project "would be costly and may achieve little".
The developments come after repeated assurances from the White House that US-Israeli attacks have depleted the Iranian armed forces, which US President Donald Trump dismissed as a "complete and total mess".
A Pentagon spokesperson previously said that the US had "destroyed up to 90% of Iran's drone, ballistic missile, and naval industrial base" and "significantly degraded" the country's ability to launch drone and missile attacks.
But Iran claims it retains large stockpiles of missiles, and footage broadcast on state TV this week claimed to show dozens of missiles at the entrance to an underground facility in southern Iran. Back in August, state TV footage also claimed to show Khordad surface-to-air missiles emerging out of a tunnel near the southern city of Bandar Abbas , external .
A MAIAR analyst also identified new construction and excavations outside tunnel entrances near the city of Qom, close to the Fordo underground uranium enrichment complex, which has been bombed by both the US and Israel multiple times.
Activity related to military assets would show that Tehran is bracing itself for further attacks by the US and Israel, said Mark Cancian, a military analyst with International Security Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
"The purpose is to better defend itself against future attacks," he said. "It also indicates a priority on rebuilding military capability rather than rehabilitating the economy."

items.title: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
items.summary: Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat election victory would mean slower AI development.
items.content:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.
Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
Pierre BaquÃ©, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.
"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.
"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September .
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

items.title: Judge blocks construction of Trump's massive arch after federal agency approval
items.summary: The Trump administration had hoped the construction of the 250-foot arch could begin as early as this week.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Protesters demonstrate against Trumpâs proposed arch
By Nardine Saad Â  and Â  Isabella Jewell ,Â  Reporting from Memorial Circle
A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of US President Donald Trump's "triumphal arch" in the nation's capital.
US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch in Washington which the Trump administration had said could begin this week.
Earlier on Thursday the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to allow construction of the planned 250ft (72m) arch.
Trump appointees on the board said the arch would be a fitting tribute to US history and to veterans but opponents have argued it would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery, the resting place of thousands of US soldiers and service people.
The so-called Arc de Trump - a play on the name of the famous arch in Paris, the Arc de Triomphe - is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city in his style and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.
The approval on Thursday evening came after nearly nine hours of public comment.
"The White House commends the National Capital Planning Commission's decision to fully approve President Trump's historic vision to build a much needed Triumphal Arch in Washington, DC," a White House spokesperson told the BBC in a statement.
It is not yet clear when construction of the arch could begin, as several lawsuits seek to block the project.
The White House criticised the federal court that temporarily halted construction as an "activist district court."
"We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch," the spokesperson said.
Image caption, An artist's rendering of Trump's proposed arch near Arlington Cemetery
A rendering of the project's design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty statue on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles. The phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" are inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.
A website that the White House shared on social media on Friday also shows a video rendering of the arch that shows the structure emblazoned with the words "Golden Age of America" along one side.
It refers to the structure as "The Military Triumphal Arch".
The proposed structure is sprinkled with appliques that are visually similar to the golden embellishments Trump has added to the Oval Office.
The Trump administration has also said the arch would double as a complex to store military equipment - complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones.
"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump previously wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch". He did not specify to which cities he was referring.
Mark Paoletta, the chairman of the NCPC and one of the Trump appointees, said at Thursday's meeting that the president understood "it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments".
How Trump is remaking the White House in his own image
He and other commissioners said the structure fulfils a 100-year plan to build a monumental work on Columbia Island, just as Congress and various commissions intended.
Paoletta added that the arch would honour the nation, its veterans and "provide the sacred ground of Arlington National Cemetery with the monumental gateway it deserves".
Image caption, Anne Wright is among those who are opposed to the arch
Anne Wright, who spent 29 years in the US military and also worked in the diplomatic service, told the BBC she would try to stop the construction.
"We'll tie ourselves to the bulldozer, we've got veterans in wheelchairs and we'll chain the wheelchairs to these things," she said.
Wright referenced this week's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress, saying: "[Trump's] policy of war, of ego â they've been rejected."
Fellow veteran John Pomeroy - who served in the Air Force for six years, including during the Vietnam War, and whose parents are buried at Arlington - said the arch "would lessen the solemn nature of a visit to the cemetery".
He described Trump's suggestion that the arch could store military equipment as "silly" and a "half-baked idea", arguing it would be a target for terrorist attacks.
Like Wright, Pomeroy said he would "impede construction workers as much as I can" if they came to the site to begin work.
Trump signs order preventing future presidents from changing Oval Office
Democratic Congressman Jared Huffman argued in his statement to the commission that the arch would disrupt sightlines not just of Arlington but of the Lincoln Memorial, fracturing "a view meant to underscore the unity and sacrifice of the American people, and doing that with a structure we often associate with emperors or kings who built grand arches as tributes to themselves".
"This is a tribute to Donald Trump," Huffman added.
Lawsuits have been filed against the plans, raising concerns about the environment, traffic congestion and safety. There is also a disagreement over whether congressional approval is needed to build the arch.
It is one of several construction projects Trump has proposed for the US capital. That includes at the White House, where he is facing legal challenges over the construction of a ballroom, which is estimated to cost $400m (Â£300m).
His plans to renovate a 106-year-old golf course, which he has dubbed "trash island", is also being challenged in the courts.

Stock futures explained: how Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 contracts work
Stock futures let traders hedge or speculate on the Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 nearly around the clock, and these five core concepts explain how they work
Hours before the opening bell rings in New York at 9:30 a.m. Eastern, financial news sites are already reporting whether Wall Street looks set to rise or fall. Those early readings do not come from the regular stock session, which has not started yet. They come from stock futures, contracts that keep changing hands while the main trading day for individual shares is closed.
Each one is a standardized agreement tied to the value of a stock index rather than to any single company's shares. They let a trader take a position on an entire benchmark without buying any of the companies inside it. The best-known U.S. contract families track the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq $NDAQ -100. CME $CME Group, the Chicago-based exchange operator, lists the most widely followed versions.
The three indexes are built differently. The Dow is price-weighted, so a stock's share price determines its influence. The S&P 500 is weighted by market capitalization. The Nasdaq -100 uses a modified version of market-cap weighting. Those design choices help explain why Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures do not always move in lockstep, even when they react to the same headline.
The contracts serve several groups at once. Portfolio managers use them to hedge stock holdings against a decline. Speculators use them to take a view on market direction. Because futures keep trading after the cash market closes, they also work as a price-discovery tool. They absorb earnings releases, economic data and news from abroad as it arrives.
A single premarket number leaves out much of how these contracts behave, including leverage, expiration dates and the gap that can open between a futures price and its index.
The five slides that follow cover a selection of core concepts. They explain how a stock index futures contract works, how the Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq -100 contracts differ from one another and why futures trade overnight. The last slide also covers how to read them before the open. Each slide stands on its own. A reader can go straight to the contract or question at hand.
What stock index futures are and how a futures contract works
A stock index future is a standardized contract to buy or sell the value of a stock index at a set price on a set future date. The contract is settled in cash, and no shares ever change hands.
Cash settlement is what separates index futures from buying stock. A trader holding an index futures contract does not own shares of any company in the index. The position gains or loses money based only on where the index level ends up compared with the price agreed in the contract.
Every contract carries a multiplier set by the exchange. Multiply the index level by that multiplier, and the result is the contract's notional value. That figure is the total market exposure one contract represents. A larger multiplier means each point the index moves is worth more to the contract holder.
Traders do not pay that full notional value up front. They post margin instead, a good-faith deposit held against possible losses. The exchange and the broker set the required amount, and it changes over time. The deposit covers only a fraction of the contract's value. That difference creates leverage. A modest move in the index produces a gain or loss that is large relative to the cash put up.
Hedging, speculation and price discovery are the three main purposes. A portfolio manager worried about a decline can sell index futures to offset losses in a stock portfolio without selling the shares themselves. A speculator buys or sells contracts to take a position on market direction. Prices that update with every trade give the market a running estimate of what the index is worth.
U.S. equity index futures follow a quarterly calendar. Contracts expire in March, June, September and December, on the third Friday of the contract month. A trader who wants to keep a position past expiration rolls it into the next quarter's contract before the current one expires.
A futures price rarely matches the cash index exactly. The gap reflects fair value, also called cost of carry. Fair value adjusts the index level for interest rates and expected dividends. That adjustment explains why futures can trade slightly above or below the index they track.
S&P 500 futures began trading at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange in 1982. The smaller E-mini S&P 500 contract followed in 1997.
How Dow futures work: the E-mini Dow contract and its 30 stocks
"Dow futures" usually refers to the E-mini Dow, a contract with the ticker symbol YM that trades on the Chicago Board of Trade, part of CME $CME Group. Its value equals $5 times the level of the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
That multiplier sets how sensitive the contract is to the index. Each point the Dow gains or loses changes the value of one YM contract by $5, either in the holder's favor or against it.
A smaller version exists for traders who want less exposure. The Micro E-mini Dow, ticker MYM, is one-tenth the size of the standard contract. It is valued at $0.50 times the index. Both contracts follow the same benchmark, so they rise and fall together. The difference is the dollar amount riding on each point.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average is a narrow benchmark. It holds 30 large U.S. companies. Charles Dow first published the average in 1896. It is one of the oldest stock market indexes still in use. A committee at S&P Dow Jones Indices chooses its members rather than a fixed formula. Transportation and utility companies are tracked in separate Dow averages.
What sets the Dow apart is how it counts each company. The index is price-weighted. It adds up the share prices of its members rather than their total market values. A stock trading at a higher price per share pulls the index harder than one trading at a lower price. A smaller company with an expensive stock can move the Dow more than a far larger company whose shares trade at a lower price.
This method also means a stock split can shrink a company's influence. When a company splits its shares, its share price falls. Its weight in the Dow falls with it. The index relies on a figure called the Dow divisor. That divisor is adjusted after splits and membership changes so the index level stays continuous.
The weighting explains why Dow futures can move differently from S&P 500 or Nasdaq $NDAQ -100 futures on the same day. A sharp move in one high-priced Dow stock can push YM noticeably while broader index futures barely react. The reverse also happens. A large move in a company that weighs heavily in the S&P 500 or Nasdaq -100 but sits outside the Dow can lift those futures while Dow futures lag behind.
How S&P 500 futures work: the E-mini S&P 500 and market-cap weighting
The E-mini S&P 500, ticker symbol ES, is the main futures contract tied to the S&P 500 index. Each contract is valued at $50 times the index level. It trades on CME $CME Globex, the electronic platform run by CME Group.
The multiplier ties the contract to the benchmark. When the S&P 500 rises or falls, the value of each ES contract moves with it, scaled by $50 per index point.
A smaller version is also listed. The Micro E-mini S&P 500, ticker symbol MES, is one-tenth the size of the standard contract, at $5 times the index. Both follow the same index. The difference is how much market exposure a single contract carries. The smaller contract lets a trader adjust a position in finer steps.
The index behind both contracts covers 500 large U.S. companies. S&P Dow Jones Indices maintains it. Companies are weighted by market capitalization, the total market value of their shares. The index uses a float-adjusted version of that measure, which counts only shares available for public trading.
Under this method, bigger companies carry more weight. A company's share price on its own does not decide its influence. A company with a modest share price but a very large total market value counts for more than one with a high share price and a smaller total value. That separates the S&P 500 from the price-weighted Dow.
The weighting shapes how S&P 500 futures behave. A sharp move in one of the largest companies shifts the index more than a move of the same percentage in a smaller member. A price swing in ES therefore leans most heavily on the biggest U.S. companies by market value.
Breadth is the index's other defining feature. The S&P 500 includes companies from all 11 sectors of the Global Industry Classification Standard, from information technology and health care to energy and utilities. That spread makes it a common reference for the U.S. stock market as a whole. News reports frequently cite ES as a gauge of how Wall Street may open.
A move in ES reflects sentiment toward large U.S. companies as a group, rather than toward one industry or a short list of stocks.
How Nasdaq-100 futures work and why they react to tech news
Nasdaq $NDAQ futures track the Nasdaq -100 index, not the broader Nasdaq Composite. The benchmark contract is the E-mini Nasdaq -100, ticker NQ, which is valued at $20 times the index level.
The two Nasdaq indexes are easy to confuse in a market report. The Nasdaq Composite includes nearly every common stock listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market, from the largest companies to much smaller ones. The Nasdaq -100 is narrower. It holds the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on that exchange. A news report that says Nasdaq futures are higher is referring to contracts on this smaller group.
Nasdaq launched the index in 1985. It is also the benchmark behind the Invesco QQQ Trust, an exchange-traded fund that holds the index's stocks. The fund and the futures contract follow the same group of companies through different instruments.
The exclusion of financial companies shapes what the index contains. Banks, insurers and similar firms are left out by design. What remains is a mix of technology, consumer, health care and industrial businesses. Large technology names carry the heaviest weight within that mix.
The Nasdaq -100 uses a modified market-capitalization weighting. Larger companies count for more, as they would in a standard market-cap index. The modification adds rules that limit how much any single company, or the largest group of companies, can dominate the index. Nasdaq reviews the index's membership once a year, in December.
That tilt toward technology shapes how NQ tends to behave. Nasdaq -100 futures often react more strongly to technology news than contracts on broader or differently built indexes. Quarterly earnings from a major technology company can register more sharply in Nasdaq -100 futures than in Dow or S&P 500 futures. On a day when technology shares rise while banks and energy companies fall, Nasdaq -100 futures can be up while Dow futures are down.
A smaller version of the contract also trades. The Micro E-mini Nasdaq -100, ticker MNQ, is one-tenth the size of the standard contract, at $2 times the index. It tracks the same 100 companies with a smaller contract value per point of movement.
Why stock futures trade overnight and how to read them before the open
Equity index futures trade nearly around the clock on CME $CME Globex, from Sunday evening to Friday afternoon Eastern time. A short daily break runs from about 5 p.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern, and the contracts react to news while the regular stock session is closed.
The regular U.S. stock market session runs from 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern. Outside that window, futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq $NDAQ -100 keep trading through most of the night. Investors get a live price for the broad market during hours when the opening bell is still far off.
That schedule puts futures among the first markets where overnight news shows up in prices. Many U.S. companies report quarterly earnings after the 4 p.m. close or before the 9:30 a.m. open. Several major economic releases also land before the bell. The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the monthly U.S. jobs report and the consumer price index at 8:30 a.m. Eastern. Stock markets in Asia and Europe trade while New York is closed, too. Futures can move on any of these developments hours before individual shares change hands in regular trading.
Reading premarket futures starts with the reference point. News reports usually describe the contracts as up or down compared with the previous settlement or close. A line saying Nasdaq futures are lower means the contract is trading below that earlier mark. The figure measures movement since the last session ended. It does not predict where the market will close.
Reports often give the move in both index points and percentage terms. The percentage is the more useful number for comparing the three contracts. The Dow, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq -100 sit at very different index levels. A move of the same number of points therefore represents a different percentage change for each one.
Futures are an indicator, not a guarantee. The market open can land somewhere different from where futures pointed earlier in the morning. Fresh news can arrive in the minutes before 9:30 a.m. and shift prices again.
Overnight trading is also thinner than trading during regular hours. With fewer buyers and sellers active, a single large order can push the price further than it would during the regular session. An overnight quote can be a less complete reading of where the broader market stands.
Individual investors can trade these contracts through brokers that offer futures accounts. Futures carry leverage. Losses on a position can exceed the initial deposit placed with the broker.

Markets News, Nov. 6, 2026: Nasdaq, S&P 500 Rise as Chip Stocks Bounce Back from AI Tailspin; Major Indexes Post Weekly Losses
The Nasdaq and S&P 500 lost ground for the fourth straight week.
Credit: Spencer Platt / Getty Images Stocks recovered some ground Friday after the U.S. market endured its worst day since the height of last year's tariff-fueled tailspin.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite and the benchmark S&P 500 gained 1.1% and 0.3%, respectively, though finished well off their session highs, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 0.5% after spending much of the morning in positive territory. The major indexes plunged Thursday , with the Nasdaq falling more than 5% and recording its biggest one-day point drop ever, while the Dow shed 1,800 points to wipe out the huge gains posted in the immediate aftermath of Tuesday's midterm elections.
Despite today's gains, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted losses for the fourth consecutive week. The S&P 500 fell 2.7% for the week, its biggest decline since April of 2025, when the announcement of the Trump administration's reciprocal tariffs sent markets reeling . The Nasdaq dropped 3.4% this week, while the Dow gave up 0.9%.
The chip stocks that led yesterday's meltdown—amid fears that AI development could slow since Democrats will have a big majority in Congress and serve as governors in key states—were among the big gainers today. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) rose 3.5%, after plunging 12% yesterday. AI bellwether Nvidia (NVDA) climbed nearly 3% to pace Dow gainers, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) soared 11%, Intel (INTC) added 8%, and Micron (MU) rose 5%.
Other AI-related stocks that were hit hard Thursday also advanced today. Shares of SanDisk (SNDK), which dropped 22% yesterday to lead S&P 500 decliners, gained 3.5%, while cloud service provider Nebius (NBIS) jumped nearly 8%. Elon Musk's SpaceX (SPCX) surged 9%, after giving up 13% over the past two days on concerns that the company's government contracts and an expected merger with Tesla (TSLA) could face heightened scrutiny under Democratic leadership.
Tech sector sentiment also got a boost from the strong results posted by Cloudflare (NET), another AI investor favorite. Shares of the networking and security services provider, which reported after yesterday's closing bell, climbed 10%.
Among other post-earnings movers, shares of Airbnb (ABNB) jumped 12% after the short-term property rental marketplace boosted its guidance. Shares of health insurer Humana (HUM) and biotech company Moderna (MDNA) each gained 5% after their earnings reports, while DraftKings (DKNG) plummeted 21%.
While uncertainty about the AI trade was top-of-mind today, investors were also keeping a close eye on a key economic data release this morning. The October jobs report showed that hiring picked up significantly in October, while the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. The numbers will factor into the Fed's decision-making on interest rates, amid expectations the central bank will hike its key rate again in the coming months.
In other markets, WTI crude oil futures held steady around $90.50 per barrel, while gold futures fell nearly 1% to $4,075 an ounce, and bitcoin traded at $75,800, little-changed from yesterday afternoon's levels. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which affects interest rates on consumer loans, ticked higher to 4.86%.
