We invest to turn our money into more money. For some of us, that can mean leaning as far toward the reward side of the "risk/reward" equation as possible—but sometimes it means playing defense, too.
How do you do that? There are lots of ways, from high-level portfolio allocation—shifting your mix of stocks and bonds, for example—to specific products. In a recent edition of Value Add: Investing Ideas, we examined funds investors can use to adjust their portfolios while staying within the boundaries of the S&P 500, a list of America's top companies, to tackle goals from income to downside protection.
The notion is of particular interest today. We're in a moment where many investors are now dialing back on, or at least reconsidering, some of the tech-oriented bullishness that has powered big gains for years.
Just look at the recent performance of some of the S&P 500's sectors: In the past month , consumer staples and real estate have been winners, while the more tech-forward have pulled back. This week's rather astonishing turn away from the AI trade, which fired up just a day after a post-midterms rally, illustrates the idea clearly.
Individual stock picks can be part of a defensive strategy too. Investors may trade the potential for big and fast gains for forms of protection—slower-but-steadier returns, dividends, and strength across the financial statements—when they suspect that reaching for outperformance isn't wise at a given moment.
To read Crystal Kim's analysis of a stock that might be about as defensive as they come—and why it passed our sniff test—subscribe to Value Add .
It's time to start saying "Bon Voyage" to the Cybertruck.
Elon Musk early Friday on X said Tesla (TSLA) would wind down production of the pickup truck next year to open factory space for Cybercabs. Though the truck was never a big seller by Tesla standards, with lifetime delivery estimates in the five digits since late 2023 , the move stands to have some significance to the business, since Tesla has said its Texas site splits manufacturing capacity between the vehicles down the middle
In that sense, the decision commits the company further to Musk's stated goal of transforming Tesla from a company that mostly makes autos for people to drive to one largely concerned with the expected next phase of mobility. Autonomous Cybercabs are a big part of that plan. (The CEO has said its high-end Roadster will one day likely be the only drivable Tesla .)
Credit: Joan Valls / Urbanandsport / NurPhoto via Getty Images But the coming departure of the Cybertruck, a big metallic slice of a vehicle, is also something of a cultural moment. Love or hate its silhouette, the truck— the "premium" version of which currently lists online for around $92,000—is instantly recognizable on the road to a degree nearly unmatched. "Apart from the Cybertruck, our cars look pretty normal," Musk said last year.
"The Cybertruck's awkwardly angular, in-your-face, stainless-steel-clad exterior proved controversial, to put it mildly," Motor Trend wrote today.
"You can buy another vehicle," Tesla said on X, "but you will spend the rest of your life thinking about me."
Caleb Silver, Investopedia's editor in chief, writes this week in Value Add , our recently launched Substack, about the steps he's taking to shield his portfolio from the recent market mayhem.
Investors are unloading AI stocks, and the Nasdaq just had one of its worst days ever, pushing it into correction territory. Worries about the sustainability of the AI-fueled gains have been growing for months, but they reached new levels this week amid fears that the pace of AI development could slow with Democrats in charge in Congress and in key statehouses.
Fortunately, my wife and I have been building a fortress around our portfolio with a bunch of stocks that I hadn't even heard of until recently. That may sound counter-intuitive and in direct opposition to the time-honored maxim of "knowing what you own," but the recent tech sell-off has put us on defense. Our wealth advisor has been making these trades in accordance with our rules-based approach to investing, and we have put our trust in him and his firm's investment committee to protect and grow our portfolios.
We've been selling chunks of our Big Tech and AI portfolio since early September. I've written in the past about how my wife and I adhere to a rules-based portfolio strategy that we exercise through our wealth advisor. That strategy compelled us to sell up to 15% of our tech and AI-heavy ETFs such as QQQM and SPYM beginning in early September and into this week. We may yet sell more, but we'll always keep these funds as core holdings in our portfolio.
What we've been buying through our advisor is far more interesting. This week, I'll share some of those individual stocks with you - not as recommendations, but as examples of the kinds of companies we want to own in times of uncertainty like these.
You can read the full article here (subscription required).
Forecasters expected the job market to edge forward last month. Instead, jobs grew at a much faster rate.
Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics ( BLS ) said Friday, well above the 59,000 economists surveyed by Dow Jones had forecast. That's up from the 60,000 revised figure for September and the 29,000 initially reported. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%, down slightly from 4.2% in September.
BLS also upwardly revised August's job gains, suggesting hiring has been stronger than realized in recent months. Before today's release, employers had added an average of about 68,000 jobs per month since the start of the year, up from 15,000 per month in 2025.
Federal Reserve officials will be looking at Friday's report to see if the labor market can take another rate increase. Last week, the Fed held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4%, a month after raising it for the first time since 2023. Two of the 12 voters had wanted to hike rates again.
Anthropic is planning one of the most anticipated IPOs in years, but recent market conditions could affect the deal as investors reconsider the outlook for the AI sector.
Some investors are "skeptical" that the AI lab can pull off the $1.5 trillion valuation many earlier expected in the wake of this week's AI-stock rout, according to The Wall Street Journal.
A valuation closer to $1 trillion may be appropriate, according to the Journal's conversation with one investor who plans to participate in the IPO.

Credit: Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images Anthropic is expected to go public this year , while OpenAI is targeting 2027. SpaceX, the business of which has a large AI component, currently trades below the price at which it sold shares to the public.

The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq are on pace to post declines for the fourth consecutive week.

items.content:
A Ryanair aircraft at Lisbon airport in Portugal on Friday, from where a flight to Rome was affected by the latest threats. Photograph: Miguel A Lopes/EPA
A Ryanair aircraft at Lisbon airport in Portugal on Friday, from where a flight to Rome was affected by the latest threats. Photograph: Miguel A Lopes/EPA
Further bomb threats disrupt at least another 18 flights across Europe
Media organisations in Ireland and UK also affected as apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos continues
A fresh wave of bomb threats disrupted air traffic across Europe on Friday but the affected aircraft landed safely and searches revealed no explosive devices.
The latest alerts affected at least 18 flights to or from Bulgaria , Cyprus, Czechia, France, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Romania and the UK.
Danish police investigated a threat against Copenhagen airport but the airport’s management said it was operating normally.
The warnings followed separate threats on Tuesday and Thursday that forced at least 35 flights to be diverted or searched, raising questions over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers.
A number of European media outlets – including news organisations in Bulgaria, Ireland and the UK – have reported that a group claiming responsibility for this week’s threats sent an email to several outlets warning of further attacks on transport across Europe.
Danish police in attendance after renewed threats at Copenhagen airport.
Photograph: Tom Little/Reuters The latest threats affected at least nine flights to and from Prague, four flights over France , two flights en route to Sofia and a flight from Lisbon to Rome. Hungary scrambled fighter jets three times to escort civilian flights in its airspace, the defence minister, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, said on Facebook.
The affected flights had knock-on effects but were a tiny percentage – just 0.0674% – of the 26,709 flights that according to the air traffic control agency Eurocontrol were scheduled in Europe on Friday.
A separate spate of threats on Friday against media organisations in Ireland disrupted broadcasts and prompted staff evacuations and police searches of offices and newsrooms.
The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, told RTÉ Radio 1 after it resumed scheduled broadcasting that such threats had to be taken seriously and were an effort to sow fear and anxiety.
“It shows how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and undermine the normal operation of society,” said Martin, adding that European security agencies would seek to identify those responsible and hold them accountable.
The British broadcaster ⁠Sky said on Friday it had also received a ⁠security threat and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.
Earlier this week, cyber-attacks targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.
The Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it was unclear whether the hoaxes and recent cyber-attacks were “all connected”.
Police in Ireland at the RTÉ offices after a spate of threats against media organisations. Photograph: Natalia Campos/Reuters She added: “But they definitely all tell us the same thing: today, what is under attack are civilian infrastructures.”
The Nato alliance continued to monitor the situation and was working closely with allies, according to a senior Nato military official.
Investigators have said there was no evidence that hoaxes against airlines and other targets were being orchestrated by a hostile terror group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, but that inquiries were continuing.
Several European media outlets in Bulgaria, Ireland, the UK and elsewhere reported that a group claiming responsibility for this week’s threats warned in an email of further actions against transport across Europe.
“This is only the beginning,” it reportedly said. The Guardian has chosen not to reproduce the email in full, given its unsubstantiated claims.
Some of the threats on Thursday were signed “fighters of the Male State”, a reference to a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016. In a Telegram post on Friday the group’s founder, Vladislav Pozdniakov, denied involvement and said the group had not existed since 2021.
Some officials suspect the waves of disruption are linked to European support for Ukraine in its war against the Russian invasion.
Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, said authorities needed more time to identify culprits but that there appeared to be a pattern.
“It ⁠cannot be mere coincidence that so many incidents with exactly the same modus operandi are happening across Europe,” he told the national broadcaster TVE.
“The ​most reasonable assumption is that we are facing ​an attempt at hybrid aggression and a form ​of psychological warfare,” he said, adding that Europe must be prepared for more such challenges.
Mark Rowley, the chief of London’s Metropolitan police, urged a measured response, saying past experience with the paramilitary Irish Republican Army offered valuable lessons.
He recalled the phrase “10p terrorism”, when a hoax bomb call made from a coin-operated phone box could disrupt an entire city, forcing authorities to distinguish between genuine and false threats.
The authorities would need to adapt to an evolving threat landscape involving actors around the world, some backed by hostile states, he said.
“We are going to have to adapt to that same methodology to make sure that we don’t overreact to every message we get online,” he told BBC Radio 4.

items.title: Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats
items.summary: Scores of flights across Europe have received bomb threats this week, but no explosives have been found so far.
items.content:
Image caption, Passengers on this Aer Lingus flight to Rome were diverted to a military base in France after a bomb threat
By Sarah Rainsford Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent
The "Male State", an extremist misogynistic group named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, has denied any link to the false warnings causing flight disruption across Europe .
The comments to the BBC came as reports of more bomb scares to airlines began appearing, including on a Ryanair flight from Rome to Lisbon and a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome which was diverted to Venice.
Bomb threats were also reported to a number of high-profile Irish media organisations on Friday, prompting evacuations and a statement from the Irish government suggesting a "co-ordinated campaign of disruption".
Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.
"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"
Image caption, The message claimed that "fighters" of the "Male State" had planted explosives on two incoming flights
The group was banned in Russia in 2021 and Pozdnyakov is now thought to live abroad. It has since renamed itself in some places as "Male Legion".
The initial hoax email, seen by the BBC, was sent on Thursday at 07:21 with the subject title: warning of a threat.
It was addressed to several offices and individuals at Aeroporti di Roma (ADR), the airport managing company in Rome, as well as accounts at the city's Fiumicino airport itself. The originating email address seems to be linked to the state health services in Bogota, Colombia.
It's not clear whether other countries' airports or airlines received the same or similar threat. At least one warning made on Friday appears to have come by phone, not email.
Written in word perfect Italian, the bizarre text sent to Rome on Thursday claimed that "fighters" of the "Male State" had planted explosives on two incoming flights in an attack on Italy's "feminist regime" that would be "remembered forever".
One flight was diverted as a result - ordered to land in France â another was escorted into Rome by Italian air force jets, scrambled for the second time this week. No explosives were found on either plane, or any other that reported receiving bomb threats.
Asked why this particular email was taken so seriously, a source at ADR in Rome told the BBC that such warnings were extremely unusual. They didn't remember anything similar in recent years.
Despite the Russian group's denial, Italy's La Stampa newspaper appears in no doubt that "Male State" was behind the threats, asking in an article whether it is acting as "the regime's armed wing".
"Attacking, and being able to deny the attacks...is part of the Russian game plan," the paper writes , external .
One Telegram channel linked to Pozdnyakov is mainly filled with virulently pro-Russian messaging about the war on Ukraine and other posts highlighting problems and tensions in Europe, including recent youth protests.
The online investigation team at Bellingcat, who studied the group back in 2022, called it then a "vocal and vile online booster" of the Russian invasion, with a clear extremist far-right ideology.
As the Europe-wide hunt continues for who is behind the spate of hoax mails, and whether they are being co-ordinated - or could be the work of copycats - Italy's defence minister has warned of a "strategy to increase chaos".
Guido Crosetto noted that he had been talking of the "hybrid threat" to Europe for some years.
"It seems to me that, day after day, from incidents involving refrigerators to the blood supply in France and now these false alarms, there are those who have an interest in fuelling tensions," the minister said on Thursday, referring to a spate of recent cyber attacks that boosted supermarket fridge temperatures, destroying mountains of produce.
"Our interest is to do the opposite and ensure the country's security," Crosetto said.

items.title: Why the US midterms sparked an AI stock selloff
items.summary: Fears of more AI regulation appear to have sparked fear among investors, but  concerns about the industry have been growing for some time.
items.content:
By Theo Leggett ,Â  International business correspondent Â  and Â  Osmond Chia ,Â  Business reporter
Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check?
That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets.
The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple.
It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's midterm elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress.
A number of leading Democrats campaigned against the unhindered expansion of data centres, which have underpinned the growth of artificial intelligence.
Fears this will lead to more regulation of AI appear to have concerned investors. But worries about the industry's prospects have been growing for some time.
The release of Chat GPT by Open AI in late 2022 is widely seen as having generated massive public and corporate interest in the practical uses of AI. It also sparked a modern-day gold rush.
Investors flocked to put their money into companies producing computer chips and networking infrastructure, building data centres and providing the energy to power them, as well as developing the AI itself. The value of tech companies soared.
The boom continued into this year. Investments in AI are expected to reach $1trillion in 2026 alone according to research by Goldman Sachs. The sector has scooped up so much available cash that other industries have seen their own borrowing costs increase as a result.
But investors want returns, and in recent months concerns have been growing about whether the AI boom can produce the expected riches.
Those worries have emerged at a time when public comments from AI researchers casting doubt over the safety of artificial intelligence - even suggesting it could represent an existential threat to humanity - have been grabbing headlines and fuelling speculation that a clampdown could lie ahead.
US tech stocks edge back up after AI slowdown fears sent value of firms plummeting
These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into grassroots concerns about the expansion of data centres and their impact on local communities.
These were largely focused on the facilities' high consumption of water and electricity, which many feared would push up their household bills â as well as the noise, use of land, and general disruption associated with them.
A Gallup poll published in May showed 71% of Americans would oppose the building of a data centre in their community. The figure for a nuclear power station was 53%.
James Talarico, who won the Senate race in once staunchly Republican Texas, was one of those to respond to this scepticism.
"While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn," he said.
"We must protect Americans and establish clear, consistent laws for businesses."
With control of both houses of Congress, Democrats are now expected to challenge the president's technology agenda more vigorously, while introducing legislation which could curb the expansion of the industry.
Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against data centres, pledging a moratorium on the construction of new facilities.
Hinojosa's win could present opposition to tech multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who has moved large parts of SpaceX and Tesla's operations to the state, for years a Republican stronghold.
The Tesla boss had spent nearly $450m to back Republican campaigns in the midterms.
As the co-founder of the British-based technology firm Arm Holdings, Tudor Brown, points out, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings". If the rewards are not likely to be as great as expected, some investors will choose to sell up.
The falls seen on stock markets over the past 24 hours would appear to have been triggered by the midterm results. But concerns that tech firms have become overvalued were being expressed long before the elections.
The question now is whether this is simply the removal of froth from an over-exuberant market, or a sign that the AI rush is a bubble about to burst, with much wider consequences.
Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights thinks investors will assess whether the political shift could result in restrictions on data centre construction, energy consumption and the deployment of AI technology.
She adds there is unlikely to be an immediate widespread recovery in tech stocks as traders are likely to be more selective, favouring firms with stronger balance sheets.
Brown thinks the impact will be limited. Share valuations, he thinks, were inflated by expectations of "almost infinite AI growth", which have been followed by "a bit of a panic".
"There is a natural floor to this", he says. "After that it will reflect I think that actually there's still a lot of money being made in these companies".

Trump teases deal covering 'all of Europe' after meeting Putin envoy
The ‘Shell Bay format’ is an unlikely phrase for history to digest.
Named after a 150-acre golf course and luxury residential complex owned by Steve Witkoff, it appeared Thursday as the moniker for the next phase of the Trump administration’s effort to end the biggest conflict in Europe since the 1940s.
Witkoff’s fellow peace-envoy and property magnate, Jared Kushner, used the term in a ponderous X post on Thursday, in which he suggested a wide-ranging peace deal was needed in Europe. “For more than 30 years, Europe and Russia have struggled to establish a sustainable security framework,” he wrote .
President Trump bolstered the idea after meeting Moscow’s envoy Kiril Dmitriev at the White House, suggesting Thursday. “I can’t tell you what I discussed. But I’m just telling you, it’s going to be a big agreement,” he said. “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.”
Jared Kushner, left, and Steve Witkoff, attend a news conference in Islamabad, Pakistan, on April 12.
Three European officials contacted by CNN Friday morning did not know what Kushner or Trump were referring to. Speaking to CNN’s Jack Tapper on Friday, Ukraine’s President Zelensky said he knew few details of the proposal and warned it would not be simple.
Kushner’s post extolled five key goals: “permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.” It said NATO would be key, even if the above seems to suggest a smaller role for the alliance the United States is the irreplaceable, founding member of.
Kushner’s ambitious word-salad did not mention Russia’s invasion of two of its neighbours and two wars with Chechnya in that same post-Soviet period. Moreover, it seemed to suggest any deal would complement NATO, rather than undermine its reason for being.
Top NATO and European officials have been meeting in Brussels in the past 72 hours to discuss economic and security concerns around Ukraine, ahead of US-led talks between Russia and Ukraine next week in Abu-Dhabi. There, the US will try and re-ignite discussions on resolving the conflict . Moscow has sent Vladimir Medinsky to lead its delegation, a diplomat fond of historical lectures, whose appointment has led many to think the Kremlin seeks to turn the clock back to May 2025, when the last such talks were held. In truth, months of discussions in Miami, Abu Dhabi, Alaska, Istanbul and Geneva have proven only one thing: Moscow wants its war goals satisfied before it’ll end the war.
President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin arrive for a press conference at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, in August 2025.
But the “Shell Bay format” - not a ‘company’, ‘game’, but a bay - emerges at a time when Trump, crestfallen and wounded after the mid-terms, will soon face greater obstacles in his domestic agenda, and perhaps seek to forge his legacy in foreign policy, where he is less restrained.
Iran is a less likely candidate for defiant action, given how Trump and many top Republicans blame the war for this week’s electoral drubbing. A form of peace in Ukraine is perhaps a sweeter alternative, and maybe Trump sees, through his ongoing rapprochement and sympathy with Russian President Vladimir Putin, a way he can truly reshape the world, enrich a choice few Americans, and get the US out of bolstering cumbersome European security.
It is telling Trump met only with Russian envoy Dmitriev, despite both Kyiv and Moscow dispatching delegations to the White House to meet with the First Lady Thursday. The English-speaking, slick investor has been pushing a variety of possible business deals as the accompaniment to improving Russian-US relations, and Democrat investigators have questioned whether Trump’s inner circle may benefit from these.
A Ukrainian flag flies next to destroyed buildings in Borodianka, Ukraine, in April 2022.
The sudden return of Ukraine to Trump’s agenda has quickened pulses in European capitals. One European official told me: “we will inevitably see Trump focus on Ukraine now the mid-terms have spoken.” Most are clear-eyed about how any deal cannot simply be imposed on Ukraine - or Europe – without their consent. “Ukraine’s need for European partners (during and post-war) is greater than being forced into accepting a Russian settlement, even if Trump tries to push that”, the official said.
The risk is to morale and the mood-music of Trump’s last 18 effective months in office. The winter ahead for Ukraine – beset already in Kyiv by water, cellphone and power cuts – may be prey to further unexplained limits on US intelligence and technical assistance, as we have seen over earlier months. Europe may face heightened sabotage and grey-zone provocations from Moscow.
The risk is not that non-American NATO and Ukraine suddenly fold or accept limits to their defense. If history is any guide, 18 months is truly a short period of time, in terms of Russian diplomatic schedules, to enact any sort of deal.
What this period of possible US-Russian rapprochement threatens could be more dangerous: that Putin may interpret a US refusal to come to Europe or Ukraine’s aid , as another reason to escalate and ruthlessly pursue the battlefield result from his war of choice that five years of invasion and two years of Trump have failed to bring him.
Kushner and Trump’s talk of a deal may signify nothing. But it opens a brief window of heightened opportunity to an increasingly strained Kremlin. And that may tempt Russia’s leadership to take yet more foolhardy risks.

items.title: Miller Reportedly Told Trump to Wind Down Iran War In Pitch For Chief of Staff Job - Yahoo
items.summary: Miller Reportedly Told Trump to Wind Down Iran War In Pitch For Chief of Staff Job  Yahoo
items.content:
Stephen Miller reportedly urged President Donald Trump to end the Iran war during his interview for Susie Wiles's chief of staff position, according to reporting by The New York Times .
As part of their live updates on the White House staff shakeup, reporter Maggie Haberman wrote, "Miller's pitch for the job, according to people who heard it, was that the president needed to wind down the Iran war, a conflict that the president's core supporters viewed as a betrayal."
Haberman also revealed Friday that Trump thwarted the Times's efforts to break the story, writing, ""@tylerpager @jonathanvswan and I had reached out to the White House to request comment for a story that Trump told many people he planned to replace Wiles, and that Stephen Miller was the likely replacement. Shortly before the deadline we gave, the president posted the news."
Some Republicans blame the Iran war for the demise of the party in Tuesday's midterm shellacking, and are even calling for the ouster of Defense Department chief Pete Hegseth.
Vice President JD Vance posted to X Wednesday, "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night."
Vance added, "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
The president's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. , retweeted Vance's post , writing, "Every word of this is 100, 100, 100."
When asked about Vance's post, President Trump said, "Well, I think it's largely true, because it drove gasoline up a little bit short-term. And probably that's — that's probably it's true. But at the same time, if I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again, because long-term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon."
When asked if he still believed the conflict in Iran was worth it, Trump replied:
"I do, yeah. Well, we have to choice. I thought oil would go up a lot more. You have to choice. You have to do it. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon, or everything that you see here some day might not exist."

S&P 500 warning signal persists as tech stocks weaken
MarketsinMotion-1200×630 ©Source: The Market Link Key Takeaways
Technology stocks are losing relative momentum, while financials and utilities are beginning to improve.
Consumer staples are attracting attention as investors assess signs of a more defensive market environment.
StoneCastle's proprietary S&P 500 early-warning indicator remains negative, following previous signals ahead of periods of market turbulence.
In the November 4 edition of Markets in Motion , StoneCastle Investment Management's Bruce Campbell examines a shift in US stock market leadership, with technology losing momentum as several other sectors begin to strengthen.
Using equal-weight sector analysis, which gives every stock the same influence regardless of company size, Campbell identifies technology moving towards the lagging quadrant. Financials, meanwhile, are beginning to recover, while utilities, consumer staples and consumer discretionary stocks are showing positive relative momentum.
This article is being disseminated on behalf of StoneCastle Investment Management, a third-party issuer, and is intended for informational purposes only.
The changing sector picture coincides with a persistent negative reading from StoneCastle's proprietary S&P 500 early-warning indicator.
Campbell highlights previous signals in 2021, November 2024 and earlier in 2026, which preceded periods of market uncertainty and volatility.
One development worth watching is the improving relative performance of consumer staples. Because these companies sell essential goods, they are often viewed as defensive investments during periods of economic uncertainty.
Utilities are also showing strength, although consumer discretionary stocks, which are generally more sensitive to economic conditions, have also registered improving momentum.
That combination suggests market leadership is shifting, but not exclusively towards defensive investments.
While Campbell's indicator does not guarantee a correction, its continued negative reading raises questions about the sustainability of the broader market's momentum.

items.title: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
items.summary: One child and one young adult were killed in the crash, local authorities say, with more injured.
items.content:
Image caption, French gendarmes and rescue workers at the scene of the crash in Lent, eastern France
A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.
The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent.
The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and at least 13 others have sustained minor injuries.
French President Emmanuel Macron said his thoughts were with the victims, the injured, and their families.
In a post on X, he said the nation stood by their side and thanked the rescue teams involved.
The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".
The two people killed have been identified by authorities. However, there have been differing reports as to the age of the girl.
The prosecutor's office said it was "opening an investigation into the incident, on charges of road homicide and aggravated road traffic injuries".
The driver has been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police. French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said initial tests indicated there were no traces of alcohol or drugs in his blood.
Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.
Local mayor Cristin told BFM TV: "I arrived minutes after the accident and people were in shock.
"The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured."
Addressing weather conditions at the time of the crash, the mayor told Le Figaro "there was a bit of fog, the road was wet" but there were "no major difficulties".
Speaking to the same paper, Fabrice Pannekoucke, head of the Auvergne-RhÃ´ne-Alpes region, said: "At this stage, there are no particular explanations or interpretations that can be given."
Tabarot said the bus did not operate "exclusively on school routes" but that there were "many schoolchildren on board".
Image caption, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot (centre) arrived at the scene following the crash
French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu said the accident was tragic, and thanked the firefighters, medical teams and police who attended the scene.
Earlier, French Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray said it was "always difficult when our children are victims of accidents of this nature".
Emergency services were at the scene and medical helicopters were deployed to take victims with serious injuries to a specialised hospital.
More than 100 firefighters and 50 gendarmes were also at the scene.
The local town hall was opened to provide shelter and coordinate with emergency services, the local mayor said.
